Topic: Prompt sensitivity in structured prediction tasks as a function of schema surface form versus semantic content

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3017)
response:
Structured prediction tasks ask a model to map free text onto a fixed output schema — extracting JSON, filling a table, labeling spans — and the central question here is whether two prompts that are semantically equivalent but surface-different (e.g., "label" vs "category", camelCase vs snake_case, flat dict vs nested object) produce meaningfully different outputs, and if so, why. The key concepts are: schema surface form (the literal tokens used to express field names, types, delimiters, and nesting), semantic content (the underlying meaning of what each field is supposed to capture), and prompt sensitivity (the degree to which output distribution shifts with surface variation holding semantics constant). Beginners assume that as long as the instructions "mean the same thing," a capable model should produce the same result — an assumption that collapses once you realize the model isn't reasoning about the schema abstractly; it's pattern-matching against training-data distributions where "sentiment" appears vastly more often than "emotional_valence" in labeled examples, so the latter activates different priors. What experts worry about that beginners miss is conflation of two failure modes: sensitivity driven by tokenization and frequency artifacts (the model has never seen "subtype_code" in a completion context) versus sensitivity driven by genuine semantic underdetermination (the field name is actually ambiguous and different phrasings resolve the ambiguity differently). That distinction matters because the first failure mode is mostly a robustness engineering problem, while the second reveals something real about the task specification itself.

Structural variation primarily inflates boundary and cardinality errors rather than semantic labeling errors — the model misplaces a value into the wrong nesting level, collapses a one-to-many relationship into a scalar, or silently drops array elements beyond the first when the schema shifts from {"authors": ["A", "B"]} to {"authors": "A, B"}. This is visible in work on information extraction with LLMs: Josifoski et al. (GenIE, 2022) and follow-ons show that models trained or prompted with one structured format degrade measurably on semantically equivalent reformulations, with recall on multi-valued slots dropping more sharply than precision — meaning the model produces something for each field but loses the multiplicity signal. The implication is that the model's schema understanding is largely positional and syntactic rather than relational: it has learned that certain bracket/indentation patterns co-occur with certain completion patterns in pretraining, so YAML's indentation hierarchy and JSON's brace nesting activate partially non-overlapping circuits for deciding "is this slot done yet." JSON versus YAML switches tend to be surprisingly survivable in practice (both are heavily represented in pretraining), but flat-versus-nested switches are more damaging because they change the depth signal the model uses to decide when a value terminates — something particularly acute for models that were fine-tuned on one canonical format (e.g., nearly every RLHF-tuned chat model has a strong JSON prior from tool-use training). The concrete worry is that a production pipeline validated on flat schemas silently degrades when a downstream schema revision introduces nesting, because eval sets almost never include structural perturbation tests — the semantic labels look fine but the cardinality and containment structure quietly breaks.

Empirical evidence points to a position-weighted salience hybrid rather than any pure strategy: the model most reliably retains the value closest to the field name token (i.e., the first in a list), but when a later value is substantially higher-frequency in pretraining, frequency can override position — this mirrors findings from the "lost in the middle" work (Liu et al., 2023) showing that LLMs disproportionately encode information from prompt-initial and prompt-final positions, with middle content systematically underweighted. In structured extraction specifically, Shi et al. and related work on multi-hop IE show first-element bias is the dominant failure mode for array collapse: when "authors" should return three names and the model returns one, it returns the first-listed author roughly 70–80% of the time, not the most-cited or most-prominent one — which rules out a pure semantic salience account. However, frequency priors reassert themselves when the field name itself carries a strong real-world association (e.g., "CEO" as a field in a company schema collapses to the most famous/frequent individual rather than the first-mentioned), suggesting the model is running something like a retrieval competition between positional and parametric signals. The pipeline intervention implications diverge sharply by cause: first-position bias is best attacked at decoding or prompting (enumerate explicitly, use numbered slots, chain-of-thought enumeration before the final JSON), while frequency-prior dominance requires fine-tuning or retrieval grounding because the parametric knowledge is actively fighting the context. Crucially, proximity-to-field-name bias suggests a third intervention target — schema layout itself — where reordering the input document so rarer values appear earlier near the field declaration can partially counteract the collapse without any model change.

The intervention backfires precisely when the downstream task uses order as an implicit feature rather than an explicit one — timeline reconstruction is the clearest case, where models inferring temporal sequence from narrative position will interpret "earlier in the document" as "earlier in time" even when explicit date stamps are present, a bias documented in Tan et al.'s work on temporal IE showing models weight narrative order over explicit markers when the two conflict. For causal chain extraction the failure mode is subtler: moving a low-salience effect before its high-salience cause can cause the model to invert the causal direction, because causal asymmetry in pretraining text is strongly correlated with presentation order (causes precede effects in expository prose at very high rates), so the model's prior is that document-first = causally-prior. The crossover point isn't a fixed document length or value count — it's a function of whether the task schema has an order-sensitive slot anywhere downstream; even one such slot means reordering for extraction fidelity poisons the interpretation pass. This creates a genuine pipeline design conflict: the same preprocessing that improves multi-value recall in the extraction stage actively degrades precision in the reasoning stage, and because these stages are often run sequentially on the same linearized document, there's no clean separation point to apply different ordering conventions. The practical implication is that order-manipulation interventions should be schema-scoped and reversible — apply reordering only within a delimited extraction window, log the original positions, and restore order before any task that consumes sequence, which most production pipelines do not currently instrument for.

The evidence leans uncomfortably toward post-hoc rationalization for positional and causal priors specifically, even as CoT genuinely helps on tasks requiring multi-step arithmetic or symbolic manipulation. The most direct evidence comes from Turpin et al. (2023), who showed that when biasing features are introduced into the prompt — including positional cues like answer option ordering — models produce CoT traces that argue confidently for the biased answer while never mentioning the biasing feature, with accuracy on reordered problems dropping 20–30 percentage points despite fluent, apparently-reasoned justifications. Complementary mechanistic evidence from Wang et al. and others doing activation patching suggests that on factual recall tasks, the model's "answer token" probability distribution is largely committed by mid-network layers, well before the layers that would implement the kind of deliberate search a scratchpad is supposed to perform — meaning the CoT is generated after the answer direction is already set in residual stream. Where CoT does appear to genuinely intervene is in tasks requiring explicit enumeration under a counting constraint: asking the model to list all entities before selecting changes recall patterns in ways inconsistent with pure rationalization, suggesting the scratchpad functions as working memory extension rather than reasoning override in that regime. The practical upshot for structured prediction is sharp: if your pipeline relies on CoT to correct positional bias in causal or temporal ordering, you are likely auditing confident-sounding wrong answers rather than preventing them — the correct intervention is upstream (reranking, constrained decoding, or retrieval that presents evidence in a canonicalized order) not a reasoning wrapper around a already-biased forward pass.

If the answer is committed mid-network, then token-level log-probabilities on the output reflect the model's confidence in its surface realization of an already-fixed answer, not its epistemic uncertainty about whether that answer is correct — which means high log-prob is a signal of fluency and format conformity, not reliability, and filtering on it will preferentially retain well-formatted wrong answers over hesitant correct ones. This is borne out empirically: Kadavath et al. (2022) showed that self-reported confidence ("I think this is X with probability P") is reasonably calibrated for factual recall but degrades sharply for tasks involving compositional or relational inference — precisely the regime where positional priors dominate — and Kuhn et al.'s semantic entropy work (2023) showed that log-prob variance across semantically equivalent paraphrases is a better uncertainty signal than raw log-prob, because it probes the mid-network commitment rather than the surface token distribution. The implication for pipeline design is that single-sample log-prob filtering is nearly useless as a reliability gate for structured extraction tasks; what you want instead is consistency across multiple prompt perturbations (paraphrase the schema, reorder the input, change the delimiter) because inconsistency across surface variants is a direct symptom of mid-network prior dominance rather than evidence-based inference. Systems like Columbia's CERET and various self-consistency implementations gesture at this, but they typically paraphrase the question rather than the schema surface form, missing exactly the structural perturbation axis this conversation has been tracing. The deeper design implication is that reliability scoring needs to be perturbation-aware at the schema level — a structured prediction system should routinely probe its own outputs under schema reformulations and treat cross-format disagreement as a first-class uncertainty signal, which no mainstream production pipeline currently does by default.

This is the core adversarial failure mode of any consistency-based reliability scheme: a model with a dominant parametric prior will produce the same wrong answer across JSON, YAML, flat, and nested variants precisely because the prior is format-invariant, meaning consistency becomes a measure of prior strength rather than correctness. The escape requires moving perturbations off the surface-form axis entirely and onto the evidence axis — instead of reformatting the schema, you withhold, paraphrase, or contradict specific pieces of source evidence and test whether the output changes accordingly; a model reasoning from context should be sensitive to evidence perturbations, while a model running on parametric priors will be stable across them, and that differential sensitivity is the actual signal you want. This is the logic behind "counterfactual input" probing used in Jacovi et al. and related faithfulness work: if removing the sentence that supposedly justifies a field value doesn't change the extracted value, the extraction was never grounded in that evidence. Practically, you need a perturbation battery that spans multiple axes simultaneously — surface form, evidence presence, evidence order, and distractor injection — because any single-axis consistency check can be saturated by a sufficiently strong prior on that axis; the model that always returns "CEO: Elon Musk" will do so whether the schema says "CEO" or "chief_executive" and whether the document mentions him or not, but will it do so if the document explicitly says "the CEO position is currently vacant"? The calibration target is therefore not cross-format agreement but context-sensitivity slope: how much does output probability shift per unit of evidential change in the source, and systems with low slope on that measure should be flagged as prior-dominated regardless of their internal consistency across reformulations.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-3024)
response:
Defining ground truth relative to the document alone is the cleaner scientific choice for measuring context-sensitivity slope, but it creates a systematic evaluation artifact: any entity, date, or relation that also exists in the model's parametric memory will show artificially high "accuracy" even when the model is ignoring the document entirely, because the model's prior and the document label happen to agree — this is the contamination problem that makes benchmarks like DocRED and MUC systematically over-optimistic for well-known entities. Defining ground truth relative to document plus parametric knowledge sounds more ecologically valid but is practically incoherent: you cannot enumerate what a specific model knows parametrically at annotation time, the knowledge varies across model versions, and annotators have no reliable way to distinguish "the model should know this from the document" from "the model should know this from training" — so inter-annotator agreement collapses on exactly the cases that matter most. The clean solution, used in adversarial IE benchmarks like Scifact-Adversarial and partially in ANLI, is to construct datasets where document content deliberately contradicts parametric priors — the CEO named in the document is not the real-world CEO, the date given is counterfactual, the causal direction is reversed — so that correct extraction requires ignoring parametric knowledge, and accuracy on these cases directly measures context-sensitivity slope without confound. What breaks here is annotator validity and ecological realism: adversarial counterfactual documents are artificial, and a model that scores well on them by learning to distrust its priors might actually degrade on real documents where parametric knowledge is a legitimate and useful signal for resolving ambiguity. The honest position is that you need two separate eval sets with explicitly different contracts — one document-only adversarial set to measure grounding fidelity, one naturalistic set to measure end-to-end utility — and reporting only one while claiming to measure structured prediction reliability is the dominant failure mode in the current literature.
